bib.title: A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 119

question: What components of a contrastive self-supervised framework (augmentation, projection head, loss, batch size, training length) make learned visual representations good, and how far can a simple version go without specialised architectures or a memory bank?
hypothesis: Composition of augmentations, a nonlinear projection head, a normalized temperature-scaled loss and large batches/long training together make a simple contrastive framework outperform prior self-supervised methods (stated as findings; the paper does not phrase them as a prior hypothesis).
contributions: Composition of data augmentations (esp. random crop + color distortion) is crucial, and contrastive learning needs stronger augmentation than supervised learning
A learnable nonlinear projection head between representation and loss substantially improves representation quality
NT-Xent loss with l2 normalization and tuned temperature beats logistic and margin losses
Contrastive learning benefits from larger batch sizes, longer training and bigger networks more than supervised learning
New state of the art in self-supervised, semi-supervised and transfer learning on ImageNet at the time

method.summary: SimCLR: two random augmentations of each image go through a shared ResNet encoder f and a 2-layer MLP projection head g; the NT-Xent loss treats the other 2(N-1) in-batch views as negatives. The head is discarded after pretraining and the encoder representation h is evaluated by linear probe, fine-tuning on 1%/10% labels and transfer to 12 datasets.
method.task: self-supervised visual representation learning (ImageNet pretraining, linear evaluation, semi-supervised, transfer)

datasets.name: ImageNet ILSVRC-2012
datasets.split: unlabeled pretraining on train set; linear eval and fine-tuning on labels; 1% (~12.8 img/class) and 10% (~128 img/class) class-balanced label subsets (Zhai et al., 2019 / tfds imagenet2012_subset); inference: resize to 256x256, single center crop 224x224
datasets.preprocessing: Inception-style random crop (area uniform 0.08-1.0, aspect 3/4-4/3) resized to 224x224, flip p=0.5, color distortion (jitter p=0.8, drop p=0.2, strength 1 default), Gaussian blur p=0.5 (sigma in [0.1,2.0], kernel 10% of image size)

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.preprocessing: first 7x7 stride-2 conv replaced by 3x3 stride-1, first max-pool removed; Inception crop resized to 32x32, color distortion strength 0.5, no blur

datasets.name: 12 transfer datasets (Food-101, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Birdsnap, SUN397, Stanford Cars, FGVC Aircraft, VOC2007, DTD, Pets, Caltech-101, Flowers)
datasets.split: creator-specified validation sets where given, otherwise held-out subset of train for hyperparameter tuning, then retrain on train+val; DTD and SUN397 first split only; Caltech-101 30 images/class train, rest test
datasets.preprocessing: resize shorter side to 224 (bicubic) and center crop 224 for linear eval; 256 shorter side then 224 center crop at fine-tune test time

models.name: SimCLR ResNet-50 (1x,2x,4x)
models.architecture: ResNet-50 encoder, h = output of average pooling (2048-d at 1x); projection head z = W2 ReLU(W1 h), output 128-d by default

other.global_BN: BN mean/variance aggregated over all devices

other.epochs: 90 for main comparison; 1000 with same strong augmentation for transfer baselines

training.objective: NT-Xent: l(i,j) = -log exp(sim(zi,zj)/tau) / sum_{k!=i} exp(sim(zi,zk)/tau), averaged over both (i,j) and (j,i) pairs in batch
training.lr: 4.8 (= 0.3 x BatchSize/256) at batch 4096; square-root scaling 0.075 x sqrt(BatchSize) also studied
training.lr_schedule: linear warmup then cosine decay without restarts
training.batch_size: 4096 default (256 to 8192 main sweep; up to 32768 in Fig B.2)
training.epochs: 100 default for ablations; 1000 for state-of-the-art models; up to 3200 in Fig B.2
training.hardware: Cloud TPUs, 32 to 128 cores depending on batch size
training.compute: With 128 TPU v3 cores, ~1.5 hours for ResNet-50 at batch 4096 for 100 epochs
training.wall_clock: ~1.5 hours (ResNet-50, batch 4096, 100 epochs, 128 TPU v3 cores)
training.seeds: Fig 9 and B.1: each bar a single run; Fig B.7: averaged over 3 runs with different learning rates

other.temperature: 0.5 best on CIFAR-10 among {0.1,0.5,1.0}; Table 5 on ImageNet: 0.1 gives 64.4 top-1
other.negatives: 2(N-1) per positive pair; batch 8192 gives 16382 (printed 16382 in text)
other.other_loss_tuning: lr {0.01,0.1,0.3,0.5,1.0}; margin {0,0.4,0.8,1.6}; logistic temperature {0.1,0.2,0.5,1.0}; negatives from one view only
other.linear_eval: Nesterov momentum, batch 4096, lr 1.6 (0.1 x BatchSize/256), 90 epochs, no warmup, random crop+flip only, no weight decay
other.finetune_semi: Nesterov momentum 0.9, batch 4096, lr 0.8 (0.05 x BatchSize/256), no warmup, no regularization, 60 epochs for 1% labels, 30 epochs for 10%
other.finetune_transfer: 20,000 steps, batch 256, SGD Nesterov 0.9, lr grid 7 log-spaced in [1e-4,0.1], weight decay grid 7 log-spaced in [1e-6,1e-3] plus none; random-init baselines 40,000 steps
other.transfer_linear: l2-regularized multinomial logistic regression, L-BFGS, 45 log-spaced l2 values in [1e-6,1e5]

inference.samples: single run per configuration in most figures; no seeds reported for tables

metrics.definition: top-1, mean per-class accuracy or 11-point mAP (VOC2007) per dataset protocol; significance by permutation test (100,000 samples)

eval.protocol: Linear evaluation protocol; single runs; permutation test (p>0.05 not significantly worse) for transfer, which ignores run-to-run training variability

limits: Authors concede max performance not reached in 100 epochs; ablations use 100 epochs, which may not transfer to full convergence (footnote 3)
Fig 9 and B.1 bars are single runs; no variance for ImageNet results
Permutation test ignores run-to-run training variability (App B.8.1)
Need large batches (up to 8192) and many TPU cores; compute costly
Gap to supervised remains for narrow ResNet-50 (69.3 vs 76.3 on ImageNet) and on all 12 transfer datasets with linear eval
Hypotheses for why the projection head and color distortion help are conjectures, supported by Table 3 and Fig 6 only
Comparison table rows from other methods differ in architecture, epochs and augmentation (Table C.1)
Results are for ImageNet-era ResNets; later methods are not covered
